Please leave your feedback about new [mini.files](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/readmes/mini-files.md) module here. Feel free to either add new comment or positively upvote existing one.

Some things I am interested to find out (obviously, besides bugs):

- Are configuration and function names intuitive enough?
- Are default values of settings convenient for you?
- Is documentation and examples clear enough?

Thanks!

Using `h/l` to go back and forth between directories or open files prevents the user from navigating the cursor around the name of the entry, somewhat limiting the ability to use the full vim editing paradigm.

Like if i have a filename `will-rename.lua` and I want to change it to `will_delete.lua`, I kind of expect to be able to do `5lcedelete`. Actually I just realized `w,e,b,f,t` still work so maybe its not so bad, but it is something I ran into because my first instinct was `lllllce` but that just opened the file. 

This can be fixed on my end by changing the mappings, but intuitive defaults are important too. Maybe something like `h,l` at the beginning and end of the line will enter or exit the directory but otherwise you can move around as normal?

I don't know, feel free to disregard but I just thought I'd point out my thoughts

Nice work on this plugin! I like the column-style navigation and the minimalism. You managed to pack a lot of features into a relatively small amount of very clean code!

This sort of file explorer is of particular interest to me, so I kicked the tires and wanted to report some bugs with file operations. For common cases everything works as expected, but there are a few edge cases that produce unexpected, and sometimes destructive, behavior.

#### Rename cycles
* Create `a.txt` and `b.txt`
* Rename `a.txt -> b.txt` and `b.txt -> a.txt`
* Result: one file is lost (note, this example happens with cycles of any length

#### Delete then recreate
* Create `a.txt`
* Delete `a.txt`, then make a new line with `a.txt`
* Sync changes
* Result: `a.txt` is deleted and a new one is not created

#### Delete inside moved dir
* Create `a/b.txt`
* Rename `a -> c` and delete b.txt
* Sync changes
* Result: `c/b.txt` still exists

#### Delete and replace
* Create `a.txt` and `b.txt`
* Delete `a.txt` and rename `b.txt -> a.txt`
* Sync changes
* Result: both files deleted

#### Copy then create inside dir
* Create `a/`
* Copy `a/ -> b/`. Create `b/c.txt`
* Sync changes
* Result: `a/c.txt` exists and `b/` is empty

#### Moving nested subdirectories
* Create `a/b/c/d.txt`
* Move `a/b/c/ -> c/`. Move `a/b/ -> b/`
* Sync changes
* `b/c/d.txt` exists but `c/` does not (it's still under `b/`)

@stevearc, thanks **a lot** for these use cases.

> Rename cycles

Yes, handling this might be a problem.

> Delete then recreate

> Delete inside moved dir
> Delete and replace
All of these might be solvable by altering order in which file operations are done. But to be fair, confirmation dialog says what it will do to explicit paths and user can decline making actions.

> Copy then create inside dir

Yes, this happens because 'b/' is not created at that point and is recognized as 'a/', so file is created as 'a/c.txt'.

> Moving nested subdirectories

Moving inside itself (meaning inside its descendant) is [not allowed](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/4b0881b9fa22ddce26ba30cdf3711226e89ba81f/doc/mini-files.txt#L282). Or I didn't understand the example.

------

All in all, beside "Rename cycles" and "Moving nested subdirectories", every other case can be solved by a more frequent synchronization. Which I think is the preferred course of action right now.

**Edit**: @stevearc, I only now realized who you are and the reason of "This sort of file explorer is of particular interest to me". Thanks so much for constructive feedback :)

> Very nice plugin! One suggestion, is it possible to provide a toggle open/close functionality, basically if open -> toggle would close the view and vice versa

It is possible, yes. At the moment I think using either explicit `q` to close it or `L` to close after opening file is more ergonomic. I'll think about it.

Edit 2: recipe for focusing current file and showing the working directory

```lua
local name = vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(0)
MiniFiles.open(name)

if name ~= '' then
	local depth = -2
	local _, init = name:find(vim.pesc(vim.loop.cwd()))
	while init do
		depth = depth + 1
		init = name:find('/', init + 1)
	end

	for _ = 1, depth do MiniFiles.go_out() end
	for _ = 1, depth do MiniFiles.go_in() end
end
```

```lua
local go_out_with_count = function()
  for _ = 1, vim.v.count1 do
    MiniFiles.go_out()
  end

  pattern = 'MiniFilesBufferCreate',
  callback = function(args)
    vim.keymap.set('n', 'h', go_out_with_count, { buffer = args.data.buf_id })
  end,

```

EDIT: Okay I'll stop spamming this thread. Here's my implementation of creating a split, moving the cursor to the new window, closing the explorer, and only executing the command if the entry is a file. I also modified the `desc` so that it shows up as "split vertical/horizontal" in the help menu:
```lua
local map_split = function(buf_id, lhs, direction)
    local minifiles = require 'mini.files'

    local rhs = function()
        -- Noop if the cursor is on a directory.
        if minifiles.get_fs_entry().fs_type == 'directory' then
            return
        end

        -- Make a new window and set it as target.
        local new_target_window
        vim.api.nvim_win_call(minifiles.get_target_window(), function()
            vim.cmd(direction .. ' split')
            new_target_window = vim.api.nvim_get_current_win()
        end)

        minifiles.set_target_window(new_target_window)
        -- Go in and close the explorer.
        minifiles.go_in()
        minifiles.close()
    end

    local desc = 'Split ' .. string.sub(direction, 12)
    nmap(lhs, rhs, { buffer = buf_id, desc = desc })
end
```

I was able to reproduce this issue but only with 'bufferline.nvim'. The reason this is happening is indeed tied with how bufferline "closes" the buffer. By default it uses `bdelete!` which "unloads the buffer from memory and deletes from buffer list" (`:h :bdelete`). But this doesn't really **deletes** buffer but merely makes it unlisted (try executing `:buffers!` after deleting one and see that it is still there but with `u` prefix).

There is another way to "really delete the buffer", which is `:h :bwipeout`. I personally use it in may daily workflow.

I suggest you solve this by using different closing command in 'bufferline.nvim' or indeed using some other "buffer-closing" plugins (*cough* [mini.bufremove](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/readmes/mini-bufremove.md) *cough*). Here is how to configure 'bufferline.nvim' to solve this:
```lua
require('bufferline').setup({
  options = { close_command = 'bwipeout! %d' },
})
```

The reason you saw this happening with 'mini.files' is because when opening file it tries to reuse existing buffer (and not mindlessly calling `:edit` which might have some side effects). As the buffer was still there, it became current but still unlisted (thus not showing in bufferline).

(Side note: windows and buffers are different things. In my early days of Neovimming, reading `:h windows-intro` helped me grasp some of these fundamentals)

Maybe an argument to `go_in` that sets the buffer as `listed` could be useful? I could see this happening with other tablines as well (even barbar potentially, if used in certain ways), as `:bdelete` is used pretty commonly.

Then again, playing with `buflisted` can be unwise as it can be set by users/plugins for a specific reason. It would also be pretty easy for a _user_ to overwrite `MiniFiles.open` to do that.

---

Edit: example

```lua
local old_go_in = MiniFiles.go_in
function MiniFiles.go_in()
	old_go_in()
	if MiniFiles.get_fs_entry().fs_type == 'file' then
		vim.schedule(function() vim.api.nvim_buf_set_option(0, 'buflisted', true) end)
	end
end
```

`:bdelete` does have its advantages (if you need to go back to that file during your current session, since buffer-local settings are preserved, marks are kept, etc), though "patching" also has its *dis*advantages (e.g. manually unlisted buffers will become listed again when opening them through `mini.files`). 

I'd wager it's probably better to configure other plugins, unless you come across one which can't be configured to use `:bwipeout` (in which case there isn't much of an alternative to patching, outside of opening an issue with that repository).

Yes, patching global table is not good. I did only slightly updated that example without big picture. Here is how I'd handle this in real config:
```lua
local minifiles = require('mini.files')

local go_in = function()
  minifiles.go_in()
  if minifiles.get_fs_entry().fs_type == 'file' then
    local buf_id = vim.api.nvim_win_get_buf(minifiles.get_target_window())
    vim.bo[buf_id].buflisted = true
  end
end

minifiles.setup({ mappings = { go_in = '' } })

vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('User', {
  pattern = 'MiniFilesBufferCreate',
  callback = function(args) vim.keymap.set('n', 'l', go_in, { buffer = args.data.buf_id }) end,
})
```

But I'd better reserve to using `:bwipeout`. To me this **is** what people usually expect from "delete buffer".

@MariaSolOs, that is an interesting question. Here is what I've come up with after modifying code for built-in sort (assuming you still want to put directories first):

<details><summary>Sort alphanumerically</summary>

```lua
local compare_alphanumerically = function(a, b)
  -- Put directory first
  if a.is_dir and not b.is_dir then return true end
  if not a.is_dir and b.is_dir then return false end

  -- Order numerically based on digits text before them is equal
  if a.pre_digits == b.pre_digits and a.digits ~= nil and b.digits ~= nil then return a.digits < b.digits end

  -- Otherwise order alphabetically ignoring case
  return a.lower_name < b.lower_name
end

local sort_alphanumerically = function(fs_entries)
  -- Precompute extra information to allow sort ignoring case and taking
  -- numerical sorting into account
  local res = vim.tbl_map(function(x)
    local pre_digits, digits = x.name:match('^(%D*)(%d+)')
    if digits ~= nil then digits = tonumber(digits) end

    return {
      fs_type = x.fs_type,
      name = x.name,
      path = x.path,
      lower_name = x.name:lower(),
      is_dir = x.fs_type == 'directory',
      pre_digits = pre_digits,
      digits = digits,
    }
  end, fs_entries)

  -- Sort based on special order
  table.sort(res, compare_alphanumerically)

  -- Convert back to contain only necessary data
  return vim.tbl_map(function(x) return { name = x.name, fs_type = x.fs_type, path = x.path } end, res)
end

require('mini.files').setup({ content = { sort = sort_alphanumerically } })
```

</details>

> 1. Change the default behavior of `go_in` and `go_out`

I think the current default `h` and `l` mappings are here to stay. Making them configurable was introduced exactly to allow this kind of customization.

> 2. Can we introduce a way to set the initial position of the floating window as well?

I don't think so. Having initial window in the top left corner allows to show the most content both vertically and horizontally. See #382.

Yes, it *might* be possible to tweak that under some conditions (like if user wants to show only one window at a time), but that would not be officially endorsed and supported.

Nice! Thanks for sharing!

My initial thought about approaching this was something along the lines of using `vim.fn.systemlist('git check-ignore -n -v -- ' .. <all file paths>)` and then directly check if line starts with `::` for it to not ignore. Should be shorter and have lower computational complexity compared to `vim.tbl_contains(output_lines, entry.path)` inside `vim.tbl_filter()`.

I used `vim.fn.jobstart` over `vim.fn.systemlist` because in the case where there are a ton of files, it's possible the argument list would become too long (there is a max limit for argument list length on UNIX systems, I don't remember what it is off the top of my head).

The `O(n^2)` time complexity of the `tbl_contains` inside the `tbl_filter` is not ideal, but it's plenty fast enough on moderately powerful hardware. YMMV ¯\\\_(ツ)_/¯
